correctness.rationale: For normalized interval maps the norm is the essential supremum of the derivative. An increasing injective attainer must have positive minimum slope c, equal to the essential infimum of its derivative, and constant derivative c on its attaining interval. A perturbation of norm δ then satisfies c ≤ a+δ and h(f) ≤ c+δ; decreasing competitors cost at least b. For any δ>(h−a)/2, putting slope a+δ on a suitable interval and clipping slopes below a+δ elsewhere meets the bound and attains the minimum. Below distance a all competitors are strictly increasing. When h>3a, subtracting a slope just above a yields derivatives of both signs and hence a repeated value, attaining zero minimum slope. For the two-speed example, positive measure of F and relative openness and density of its complement give a and h=b. The midpoint affine slope realizes the bound for b≤3a, including equality; for b>3a every competitor within distance a is increasing strictly, has minimum slope at most 2a, and has slopes exceeding 2a on a positive-measure subset of every interval, so no interval attains that minimum.
residual_risks: Analytic review on the stated scalar interval and positive lower slope; no formal certificate or external attestation claimed.
